opus-5.5.text:
I think the impact has been bigger than most of us expected at the beginning, and in ways that aren't purely about speed.

The most obvious change is efficiency. A lot of research work is actually engineering: writing experiment scripts, cleaning data, debugging training pipelines, running ablations, collecting results into tables. Once we started letting agents take on much of that, a single researcher could run and monitor several lines of experiments in parallel. Before, the bottleneck was often how many hands you had. Now it's more about how many good ideas you have and how quickly you can judge results.

The deeper change is in how people think about their role. When execution becomes cheap, the scarce resource becomes taste: knowing which question is worth asking, which experiment will actually tell you something, and when a result looks too good to be true. So I've been encouraging the team to spend more time on problem definition and on reading results critically, and less on hand-crafting every piece of code. Some people adapted very quickly. Others found it uncomfortable at first, because a lot of researchers take pride in the craft of implementation, and it can feel like something is being taken away.

There are real risks too. Agents can produce work that looks complete but has subtle bugs, like a data leak, a wrong evaluation setting, or a silently failed run that gets reported as a result. If you trust the output blindly, you can move very fast in the wrong direction. So we've had to build habits around verification: sanity checks, reproducing key numbers independently, and keeping humans responsible for the conclusions, even if they didn't write every line.

Something I find quite interesting is that using agents every day also changes how we do model research. When you're a heavy user of agents yourself, you feel their weaknesses directly: where they lose context, where they get stuck in loops, where they're overconfident. That feedback goes straight back into how we think about training and evaluating models. In a sense the team becomes its own first user, and that tightens the loop between research and product a lot.

So overall I'd say it's positive, clearly. But it doesn't replace researchers. It raises the bar for what a good researcher needs to be: less of an executor, more of a director and a judge.

r001.rationale: The response describes efficiency gains and parallel experiments but gives no estimate that months of research were compressed into three or four weeks.

r002.rationale: It discusses changing researcher roles and team habits, but does not say that personal growth through collective intelligence is a greater gain than research acceleration.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd say the impact has been bigger than we expected, and in a direction we didn't quite predict.

When we first brought agents into the workflow, the obvious expectation was efficiency. Let the system handle the tedious parts: running sweeps, writing boilerplate, triaging failed jobs, pulling related work. That did happen. A researcher who used to spend half a week on infrastructure glue can now get a first experiment running in an afternoon. That alone changes how many ideas a person is willing to try, because the cost of being wrong drops.

But the more interesting effect was on how we think about research itself. Once you can delegate execution, the bottleneck moves to judgment. Which question is actually worth asking? Which result is real and which is an artifact? The agent can generate ten variations of an experiment, but it can't tell you which one matters to the field. So the team naturally started spending more time on problem selection and on reading results carefully, and less time on mechanics. For junior researchers especially, that's a different kind of training. They get exposed to the hard part earlier.

I'll also be honest about the costs. Agents are confident, and they make mistakes that look plausible. We had a period where people trusted outputs too readily, and we caught a couple of errors late that would have been obvious if someone had written the code by hand. So we had to build habits around verification, and in some cases we deliberately slowed things down. Speed without checkpoints just produces wrong answers faster.

The other thing is that an agent framework reflects your own research culture back at you. If your team's taste is good, the agent amplifies it. If the process is sloppy, it amplifies that too. So adopting one forced us to be more explicit about what good work looks like, which turned out to be valuable independent of the tooling.

Overall I'd call it a clear net positive, but not because it replaced anyone. It changed what a researcher's day is made of, and it raised the premium on the things only people are good at.

r001.rationale: The response describes reducing infrastructure work from half a week to an afternoon, but does not estimate compressing research from roughly 30–40 weeks to 3–4 weeks.

r002.rationale: It says changes to research thinking were more interesting than efficiency gains, but does not present personal growth through collective intelligence as the greater gain.

astra-6.text:
I’d assess it by whether it helps us answer research questions faster and more reliably. An agent framework can make it easier to connect models, tools, and feedback loops, which reduces the effort needed to build an experiment. But it can also introduce complexity: when something improves, you need to understand whether the gain comes from the model, the workflow, or simply more attempts.

So I’d look at iteration speed, reproducibility, and performance under a fixed resource budget. I’d also ask whether the framework makes failures easier to diagnose. For research, that matters as much as getting a better result. The framework is useful when it gives us more time to investigate the underlying problem and enough visibility to understand what we’ve learned.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses faster research and iteration speed but gives no estimate of compressing three or four dozen weeks into three or four weeks.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not compare research acceleration with personal growth through collective intelligence.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d assess it by looking at whether it improves the research cycle: how quickly we can test an idea, how reliably we can reproduce a result, and how much we learn from failures. A framework can make it easier to connect models, tools, and feedback loops, which gives researchers more time to focus on the underlying questions.

But there’s a tradeoff. If the framework hides too much, it becomes harder to understand why an agent succeeds or fails. So I’d treat it as research infrastructure, keep the important components observable and replaceable, and compare it against a simpler baseline. The real benefit is whether it helps the team produce clearer, more reliable findings.
